section.title: The Centurion, the Widow's Son, and the Sinful Woman
section.sectionRationale: Four scenes answer the question Luke's readers are asking: who is this Jesus? A Gentile centurion shows the greatest faith Jesus has found in Israel; at Nain Jesus halts a funeral and raises a widow's only son; He answers John the Baptist's doubt by pointing to His works and testifies to John's greatness; and at a Pharisee's table a sinful woman washes His feet with her tears while He pronounces her sins forgiven. Together they display the Savior for the outsider, the grieving, and the sinner.
section.thesis: Jesus is the promised One whose word heals across every boundary, whose compassion raises the dead, and whose authority forgives sins; the faith that amazes Him is found in a Gentile soldier and a weeping sinner, not in the religiously respectable, and to such faith He says, go in peace.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the centurion whose faith amazes Jesus; the raising of the widow's son at Nain; John's question and Jesus' testimony about John; and a sinful woman forgiven at Simon the Pharisee's table.

units.label: The faith of the centurion
units.note: such great faith, not found in Israel

verses.text: When Jesus had concluded His discourse in the hearing of the people, He went to Capernaum.
There a highly valued servant of a centurion was sick and about to die.
When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent some Jewish elders to ask Him to come and heal his servant.
They came to Jesus and pleaded with Him earnestly, “This man is worthy to have You grant this,
for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue.”
So Jesus went with them. But when He was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends with the message: “Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof.
That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to You. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.
For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.”
When Jesus heard this, He marveled at the centurion. Turning to the crowd following Him, He said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great {{pistis|faith}}.”
And when the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant in good health.

units.label: The widow's son at Nain
units.note: the Lord had compassion and raised the dead

verses.text: Soon afterward, Jesus went to a town called Nain. His disciples went with Him, accompanied by a large crowd.
As He approached the town gate, He saw a dead man being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. And a large crowd from the town was with her.
When the Lord saw her, He had {{splanchnizomai|compassion}} on her and said, “Do not weep.”
Then He went up and touched the coffin, and those carrying it stood still. “Young man,” He said, “I tell you, get up!”
And the dead man sat up and began to speak! Then Jesus gave him back to his mother.
A sense of awe swept over all of them, and they glorified God. “A great prophet has appeared among us!” they said. “God has visited His people!”
And the news about Jesus spread throughout Judea and all the surrounding region.

units.label: John's question and Jesus' testimony
units.note: are You the One who was to come

verses.text: Then John’s disciples informed him about all these things.
So John called two of his disciples and sent them to ask the Lord, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?”
When the men came to Jesus, they said, “John the Baptist sent us to ask, ‘Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?’”
At that very hour Jesus healed many people of their diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and He gave sight to many who were blind.

So He replied, “Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.
Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”
After John’s messengers had left, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind?
Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear elegant clothing and live in luxury are found in palaces.
What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’
I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John, yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”
All the people who heard this, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God’s justice. For they had received the baptism of John.
But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, because they had not been baptized by John.
“To what, then, can I compare the men of this generation? What are they like?
They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling out to one another: ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon!’
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’
But wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”

units.label: A sinful woman forgiven
units.note: her many sins are forgiven, for she loved much

verses.text: Then one of the Pharisees invited Jesus to eat with him, and He entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at the table.
When a sinful woman from that town learned that Jesus was dining there, she brought an alabaster jar of perfume.
As she stood behind Him at His feet weeping, she began to wet His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair. Then she kissed His feet and anointed them with the perfume.
When the Pharisee who had invited Jesus saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, He would know who this is and what kind of woman is touching Him, for she is a sinner!”
But Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” “Tell me, Teacher,” he said.
“Two men were debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed him five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.
When they were unable to repay him, he forgave both of them. Which one, then, will love him more?”
“I suppose the one who was forgiven more,” Simon replied. “You have judged correctly,” Jesus said.

And turning toward the woman, He said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? When I entered your house, you did not give Me water for My feet, but she wet My feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
You did not greet Me with a kiss, but she has not stopped kissing My feet since I arrived.
You did not anoint My head with oil, but she has anointed My feet with perfume.
Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much. But he who has been forgiven little loves little.”
Then Jesus said to her, “Your sins are {{aphiemi|forgiven}}.”
But those at the table began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?”
And Jesus told the woman, “Your faith has {{sozo|saved}} you; go in peace.”

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, a confident reliance that takes God at His word. The centurion's faith amazes Jesus because it rests entirely on the power of Jesus' bare word, trusting that He need only speak and it is done. The same word crowns the chapter as Jesus tells the forgiven woman that her faith has saved her.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion from deep within, literally to feel it in the inward parts. It describes a visceral, gut-level mercy. At Nain the Lord sees a widow burying her only son and is moved with this compassion, and He acts before she asks, halting the funeral and giving her son back alive.

aphiemi.gloss: To send away, release, cancel, or forgive. Used of releasing a debt and of forgiving sins, it pictures guilt lifted and carried off. Jesus says the woman's many sins have been sent away, and then speaks directly to her, 'Your sins are forgiven,' an authority the table guests recognize belongs to God alone.

sozo.gloss: To save, rescue, make whole. It covers deliverance from danger and disease and the fuller salvation of the whole person. To the weeping, forgiven woman Jesus says, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace,' so that her rescue is not merely emotional relief but true salvation received by faith.

basic.context: Four scenes press the question of who Jesus is. A Roman centurion, a Gentile, sends word that Jesus need only speak and his servant will be healed, and Jesus marvels at faith greater than any in Israel. At Nain He meets a widow following her only son's coffin, is moved with compassion, and raises the young man. When John the Baptist, in prison and wavering, sends to ask if Jesus is really the One, Jesus points to His works of mercy and honors John as the greatest of the prophets. Finally, at a Pharisee's dinner, an immoral woman weeps over Jesus' feet, and He declares her many sins forgiven and tells her that her faith has saved her.
basic.hermeneutics: Read these scenes together as Luke's portrait of the Savior for the outsider and the sinner. The centurion and the sinful woman, both on the margins, show the faith that pleases Jesus, while the respectable Simon and the doubting religious leaders miss it. The parable of the two debtors interprets the woman's tears: great love flows from knowing you have been forgiven much, not the other way around.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on faith, pistis, the trust that takes Jesus at His word, praised in a Gentile soldier and in a weeping woman. At Nain Jesus is moved with splanchnizomai, gut-deep compassion. To the woman He speaks release, aphiemi, her sins forgiven and sent away, and He tells her that her faith has sozo, saved her.
basic.typology: Raising the widow's only son at a town gate recalls Elijah and Elisha raising sons for grieving mothers, marking Jesus as the great prophet, yet greater, for He commands the dead by His own word. John the Baptist fulfills Malachi's promised messenger who prepares the way, and Jesus' list of works answers Isaiah's picture of the age of salvation.
basic.christ: Jesus heals a Gentile's servant from a distance by His word, raises the dead by His touch, and forgives sins with an authority that belongs to God alone. He is more than a prophet; He is the One who was to come, whose works fulfill Isaiah and whose mercy reaches the soldier, the widow, and the sinner. In forgiving the woman He does openly what only God can do.
basic.god: God visits His people in Jesus, as the crowd at Nain rightly senses. He is the God whose purpose the humble receive and the proud reject, who justifies the tax collectors and sinners who come to Him, and who cancels debts no one could repay. His mercy runs toward those who know their need.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 4 tell of prophets raising widows' sons. Malachi 3:1 is quoted of John the messenger. Isaiah 35 and 61 stand behind Jesus' list of works. And Luke 5:20-21 already raised the question of who can forgive sins but God alone.
basic.oneStory: The One promised through the prophets has come, and He is the Savior for the outsider and the sinner. His word crosses every boundary to heal, His compassion overturns death, and His authority forgives the guilty. The faith that receives Him is found not in the respectable but in a Gentile soldier and a weeping woman, and to such He says, go in peace.

context.literary:
Luke 7 is built as a sequence of four encounters in which each person stands at a different distance from Jesus, and the distances are not what the reader expects. The soldier never meets Him face to face, the widow never asks Him for anything, John is confined and cannot come, and the woman who does come close has no invitation. Luke sets two miracles first, then a conversation about who Jesus is, then an enacted parable at table, so that the deeds supply the evidence for the question that verse 49 finally voices aloud: 'Who is this who even forgives sins?'

There is a deliberate pairing of the first two scenes. A man's slave is rescued at the point of death, and a woman's son is rescued after it. Both rescues happen by speech, 'just say the word' in verse 7 and 'I tell you, get up!' in verse 14, and both end with Jesus giving someone back, the servant restored to his master's household and the son 'back to his mother.' Verses 18 to 23 then turn the miracles into testimony: Jesus does not argue for His identity, He tells John's men to report what they have seen and heard.

The longest unit, verses 36 to 50, is built around the hospitality list in verses 44 to 46, which Jesus recites in three matched lines, 'you did not... but she.' The parable of the two debtors in verses 41 to 43 is set like a hinge between Simon's private verdict in verse 39 and Jesus' public verdict in verses 47 to 50. Simon says 'If this man were a prophet,' and the whole scene answers him: Jesus does know who the woman is, and He knows who Simon is as well.

Notice also the framing sayings. The chapter opens with a Gentile whose faith Jesus has 'not found' even in Israel, and it closes with a woman told that her faith has saved her. Between them stand a section on wisdom in verses 31 to 35 and the sentence that the people and tax collectors 'acknowledged God's justice' while the Pharisees 'rejected God's purpose,' verses 29 and 30. Luke wants the reader to feel that responses to Jesus sort people into new groups.
context.historical:
Capernaum lay in the territory of Herod Antipas, and a centurion stationed there was most likely in the service of Antipas rather than commanding a Roman legion. He was a Gentile soldier of an occupying power, yet the Jewish elders speak up for him, which tells us something about how a foreign officer had earned a hearing in a small lakeside town. Roman soldiers were more often resented than praised. The elders' logic in verse 5, that he is worthy because he built the synagogue, is the logic of patronage. The centurion's own logic in verse 6 is the reverse: he does not count himself worthy at all. Jews would not normally enter a Gentile house without becoming unclean, which is a likely reason behind his message that he is unfit to have Jesus under his roof.

Nain was a small village in lower Galilee, south of Nazareth, and the stretch of country is the same area where the Old Testament set the Shunammite woman's story, 2 Kings 4. Burial took place on the day of death. The dead were carried on an open bier, not in a closed box, and the procession left the town for a burial ground outside the gate. Touching a bier or a corpse made a person unclean for seven days, Numbers 19:11, so Jesus' touch in verse 14 is a deliberate step across a purity boundary. A widow with no son had no legal heir and no protector, which is why Luke stresses 'the only son of his mother, and she was a widow.'

John's imprisonment is by Herod Antipas, whose reasons Luke gave at 3:19 to 20. The Baptist was held in a fortress east of the Dead Sea, according to the Jewish historian Josephus, so his messengers had a long road to travel.

At a formal dinner in a Pharisee's house, guests reclined on couches with their feet stretched out behind them, which is how a woman could stand at Jesus' feet unseen at first. In village hospitality uninvited people sometimes gathered at the edge of a banquet to watch. A woman letting her hair down in public would have been shameful, and the alabaster flask of perfume probably represented something valuable and deeply personal. The two debts, five hundred and fifty denarii, differ by a factor of ten. A denarius was roughly a day's pay for a labourer.
context.canonical:
The chapter is soaked in the Old Testament, but it also looks sideways to the other Gospels and forward into Acts. The centurion's story appears in Matthew 8:5 to 13, where Jesus adds that 'many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' Matthew 8:11. That is the Gentile mission in a sentence. Luke's own sequel shows it happening: another centurion, Cornelius, is 'devout and God-fearing,' Acts 10:1 to 2, and Peter learns at his house that God shows no partiality. Luke has already told his readers at Nazareth that Elijah was sent to a widow in Sidon and Elisha healed Naaman the Syrian, Luke 4:25 to 27, and the two miracles of chapter 7 are the Nain and Capernaum versions of those very stories.

The raising at Nain draws on Elijah at Zarephath. Both scenes begin at a town gate with a widow, 1 Kings 17:10, and both end with the same gesture: Elijah 'gave him to his mother,' 1 Kings 17:23, and Jesus 'gave him back to his mother,' Luke 7:15. The crowd's cry 'God has visited His people' picks up Zechariah's song, 'He has visited and redeemed His people,' Luke 1:68.

John's question is Isaiah's world. Jesus' list of works gathers Isaiah 35:5 to 6, the blind, the deaf and the lame, with Isaiah 26:19, 'Your dead will live,' and Isaiah 61:1, good news to the poor, the text He read in the Nazareth synagogue, Luke 4:18. The parallel passage in Matthew 11:2 to 19 shows the same scene told with different emphasis.

The woman's anointing should be kept apart from the anointing at Bethany in Mark 14:3 to 9 and John 12:1 to 8. Luke tells his own story, in a Pharisee's house, early in the ministry, and he does not name the woman. Mary Magdalene appears for the first time in the very next chapter, Luke 8:2, introduced as a new character. The forgiveness theme runs on through Luke 15 and 18:9 to 14, and through Acts 10:43 and 13:38.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote for Theophilus and readers like him who had heard the claims about Jesus and wanted certainty, Luke 1:4. This chapter gives that certainty through evidence rather than assertion. A reader who asks whether Jesus is the promised one is shown the lists of Isaiah worked out in a village street, a soldier's house and a Pharisee's dining room.

The author also meant to unsettle a reader's assumption about who is near to God. Luke seats the religiously respectable on the side of the unconvinced: the lawyers, who 'rejected God's purpose for themselves,' verse 30, and Simon, whose guest has to teach him his own hospitality. He seats the outsiders on the side of faith. Readers who were Gentiles themselves would hear that Jesus does not need them to come to Judaism first, since the centurion is not asked to convert before his servant is healed.

There is a pastoral purpose too. John's question lets every weary believer see that doubt is not the end of faith, and that Jesus answers doubt with patience and testimony. The final lines of Luke's story invite the reader to be the woman and not Simon: someone who knows what has been forgiven, and loves because of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what Jesus did on particular days for particular people. Nothing in it promises that every sick servant will be healed or every funeral stopped. Luke does give a pattern, though, that does carry forward: Jesus is moved by the sorrow of people who ask for nothing, He honours a faith that rests on His word even when it cannot see, and He receives the repentant at any cost to His own reputation.

The woman's actions are narrative, not a liturgy to copy. Nowhere does Jesus tell anyone to anoint feet or to weep at a meal. What He commends is the love behind the act and the faith it expresses. The centurion's argument from authority is likewise not a formula for prayer but an example of how to trust a word. And Jesus' rebuke of Simon is meant to reshape the reader's own posture: to ask whether we welcome sinners, and whether we have forgotten our own debt.

debates.question: Why did John the Baptist, who had pointed to Jesus, now ask if He was the One?

views.label: Genuine wavering in prison
views.case: John languishes in Herod's prison and Jesus' ministry does not look like the fiery judgment John announced; his question voices a real, honest struggle, which Jesus answers gently with evidence rather than rebuke.

views.label: Asking for his disciples' sake
views.case: Some suggest John sent his followers so that they, not John, would hear Jesus' answer and be directed to Him; the question guides the messengers to see the works for themselves.

debates.bearing: Either way Jesus points to His works of mercy that fulfill Isaiah, and blesses those who do not fall away over Him, meeting doubt with evidence and reassurance.

debates.question: Does the woman's love earn her forgiveness, or flow from it?

views.label: Love flows from forgiveness
views.case: The parable of the two debtors makes forgiveness the cause and love the response: the one forgiven more loves more; her tears are the overflow of grace already received, and Jesus finally says her faith, not her love, has saved her.

views.label: Her love shows she was forgiven
views.case: The phrase 'for she loved much' can read as evidence rather than cause; her lavish love is the visible proof that her many sins have already been forgiven.

debates.bearing: Both guard the gospel: forgiveness is received by faith, not purchased by love, and great love is the sure fruit of knowing you have been forgiven much.

study.originalLanguages:
The centurion's message in verse 7 uses an imperative that is easy to miss: eipe logō, 'say it by a word.' The healing he asks for is not ritual or touch but speech. When Jesus replies that He has not found such pistis in Israel, He uses the verb ethaumasen, 'marveled,' a word that is rare for Jesus. It shows that faith can surprise Him, and that its shape is not Jewish heritage but trust in His authority. The centurion's reasoning in verse 8, a man hupo exousian, 'under authority,' who gives orders because he stands under someone higher, is exactly what Jesus' own exousia in Luke 4:32 and 4:36 had displayed.

At Nain, Luke says Jesus was moved with compassion, esplagchnisthē, from splanchnizomai, a verb built on the word for the inner organs. It is Luke's word for the Samaritan who sees the wounded man, Luke 10:33, and for the father who sees his returning son, Luke 15:20. In all three the compassion comes first, and the action follows. Luke also calls Jesus ho kyrios, 'the Lord,' in narration in verse 13, so the title is given to Him here by the evangelist himself. The command in verse 14 is egerthēti, 'be raised,' from egeirō, the usual verb for resurrection. The crowd's verdict that God has 'visited,' episkepsato, from episkeptomai, echoes Luke 1:68 and 1:78, where the word describes God's saving intervention.

John's question uses ho erchomenos, 'the coming one,' which in the Old Testament is attached to the person who comes in the Lord's name, Psalm 118:26. His disciples ask whether to wait for someone else. Jesus' answer in verse 23 uses the verb skandalizō, 'fall away,' from skandalon, a stumbling block. A skandalon is whatever trips faith, and the blessing is promised to the one who is not tripped by Jesus' unexpected way of being the Messiah.

In the woman's story the verb for forgiveness is aphiēmi, and in verses 47 and 48 it is in the perfect tense, apheōntai: her sins 'have been forgiven,' with a result that stands. Her love shows the forgiveness; it does not purchase it. The same woman is told in verse 50, 'Your faith has saved you,' using sesōken, again a perfect, and then 'go in peace,' poreuou eis eirēnēn, an idiom that echoes the Hebrew blessing of shalom. Simon, at the table, is said to judge 'rightly,' orthōs, in verse 43, and Jesus uses his own right answer to open the trap.

Finally there is the sharp difference between two kinds of anointing in verse 46. Jesus says Simon gave no olive oil, elaion, for His head, while the woman anointed His feet with myron, perfume, a costlier thing. The woman's gift exceeds the courtesies that were due.

typology.type: Elijah raising the widow's son at Zarephath, 1 Kings 17:17-24
typology.fulfillment: Elijah met a widow at a city gate, restored her dead son, and 'gave him to his mother.' Luke tells the Nain story with the same bones: a gate, a widow, a dead son, a handing back. The crowd names the type itself: 'A great prophet has appeared among us!' But the escalation is plain. Elijah stretched himself out over the boy three times and cried to the LORD, and Elisha stretched out over the Shunammite's son and prayed. Jesus uses no prayer of intercession and no contact beyond a touch, only the sovereign command 'get up!' The type falls short in that the prophets were servants who asked God for life, whereas Jesus is the Lord who gives it.

typology.type: The messenger who prepares the way, Malachi 3:1
typology.fulfillment: Malachi promised a messenger who would prepare the way before the Lord, and Jesus names John as that figure, verse 27. In Malachi the one who follows the messenger is 'the Lord whom you seek,' who 'will suddenly come to His temple.' By applying the verse to John, Jesus implicitly identifies Himself as the one for whom the way was prepared. John is therefore the greatest of those 'born of women,' verse 28, because of his position at the turning point of the ages, but the type falls short in the same place: the forerunner stands at the door of the kingdom and does not enter into its fuller blessings the way the least who are in it do.

typology.type: The works of the age of salvation, Isaiah 35 and 61
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah pictured a day when the eyes of the blind would be opened and the lame would leap, Isaiah 35:5 to 6, and when good news would be preached to the poor, Isaiah 61:1. Jesus does not quote these verses; He points to what is happening in front of John's messengers. Prophecy has become observable, and Luke's order is deliberate, since the list climbs to 'the dead are raised' and ends with 'the good news is preached to the poor.' What fulfilment adds is the surprise that the one who brings the age of salvation leaves Isaiah's other line, the day of vengeance, for later. John expected the axe of Luke 3:9, but Jesus first brings release.

typology.type: The two debtors and the cancelled debt
typology.fulfillment: The parable of the two debtors acts as a small type of the gospel itself. A lender, who stands for God, forgives two people who cannot pay, and love grows in proportion to the sense of the debt cancelled. It echoes the Old Testament picture of God who 'forgives all your iniquities,' Psalm 103:3. The correspondence is that Jesus does openly what the lender does in the story: He says 'Your sins are forgiven,' verse 48. The limit of the picture is that the parable has no cost to the lender, and the cross shows that forgiveness cost God His own Son, Ephesians 1:7.

study.christ:
This chapter shows Christ by the authority of His word. The centurion treats Jesus as someone whose bare command carries the force of a commanding officer's, and Jesus accepts the comparison. That is a claim to a position over sickness, over death and over sin. In each scene a spoken sentence does what elsewhere belongs to God alone: 'just say the word,' 'I tell you, get up,' and 'Your sins are forgiven.'

It also shows Christ as the one who takes up uncleanness without being defiled. At Nain He touches the bier, which should make Him unclean, and the dead man lives. At Simon's table He lets a sinful woman touch Him, and Simon draws his conclusion, 'If this man were a prophet.' Luke has been showing Jesus step across the lines of ritual separation to restore people, and the pattern continues through Luke 8, where a woman with a flow of blood touches Him. Uncleanness does not pass to Him; His wholeness passes to them.

John's question is the question every reader brings, and Jesus answers by pointing to His works, not by claiming the title. That restraint matters. He is the Christ, but He is the Christ who heals before He judges, Isaiah 61:1 before Isaiah 61:2. Verse 23 then adds a note of warning: it is possible to be offended at this Jesus. The answer to the problem of John is to keep trusting the one whose methods are not ours.

Finally, the chapter points to Christ as the Son of Man who comes 'eating and drinking,' verse 34. His critics call Him a friend of tax collectors and sinners, and He does not deny it. This is the heart of the gospel. Paul says that 'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners,' 1 Timothy 1:15, and the woman at Simon's feet is the first picture in Luke of what that looks like. The cross is yet to come, but the forgiveness He gives her anticipates it. Any reading that makes Jesus a teacher of kindness and not the bearer of the debt would miss what the debtors' story needs: someone must pay.

We should guard against over-reading. The widow's tears are not a code for Israel, and the centurion is not an allegory of the church. The links hold where Luke and the rest of the New Testament make them, and the primary lesson is simple: here is a person who commands the sick, the dead and the guilty, and who is gentle with all three.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who comes to visit. The crowd at Nain says it for all of them: 'God has visited His people!' Luke has taught his readers that the verb is a salvation word, so what the villagers say more truly than they know is that God is present in this man's compassion. Whatever else we say about God has to be able to stand next to a widow's coffin. The God of Luke 7 is not detached; He draws near, and He is moved before He acts.

It shows a God who is sovereign over death. Verse 14 gives no formula and no ritual. A word is spoken and a dead man sits up and speaks. This is the God of Isaiah 26:19, who says that the dead will live, and of Psalm 68:20, who is a God of salvation and escape from death. At the same time, He is not a God who makes sorrow disappear in general. He meets one mother's grief, and the Gospel records plenty of funerals that went on. We hold both: He rules death and He is patient with His timing.

It shows a God whose justice and purpose can be rejected. Verses 29 and 30 divide the crowd into those who 'acknowledged God's justice' and those who 'rejected God's purpose for themselves.' God's purpose is not forced; it can be refused, and the refusal is costly. The tax collectors who accepted John's baptism had agreed with God against themselves, and that agreement is where the whole business of forgiveness begins.

It shows a God who forgives, and who alone has the right to. The question at the table, 'Who is this who even forgives sins?', has already been asked in Luke 5:21, and it is not answered here by denial. The text lets it stand. Only God can forgive, and Jesus forgives. The conclusion is left for the reader to draw.

He is also a God who is generous toward the poor and honest about debt. The lender in the parable forgives both debts, so grace is not limited to the one with a bigger ledger. Both debtors needed it. Simon's smaller debt is real, and the cancelled sum is as unpayable for him as for her.

For worship, the chapter teaches a particular shape of response. The woman's weeping, her kissing and her perfume are what gratitude looks like when it has no words. Worship in this chapter is not tidy. It costs something, it embarrasses the onlookers and it flows from knowing what we have been forgiven. And it ends with a word, 'go in peace,' that sends the worshipper back into ordinary life.

crossReferences.note: Elijah restores the widow of Zarephath's son, and the scene starts at a city gate and ends with Elijah giving the boy back to his mother. Luke's wording at Nain is a close echo, so the crowd's cry about a great prophet is the right instinct. The difference is that Elijah prays three times and Jesus simply commands.

Elisha raises the Shunammite's son by prayer and by stretching himself over the body. The village of Shunem lies close to Nain, which makes Luke's setting resonate. Where Elisha needed bodily contact repeated and calling on the LORD, Jesus touches the coffin and speaks once.

The prophet describes the coming salvation as the opening of blind eyes and deaf ears and the leaping of the lame. Jesus' answer to John gathers these signs and calls them to witness. The works are not random kindness; they are Isaiah's promises appearing in Galilee.

The anointed one brings good news to the poor, which is the last item in Jesus' list and the text He read at Nazareth, Luke 4:18. Putting it last tells John that his own imprisonment fits within the same mission of release.

God promises to send a messenger to prepare His way, and Jesus cites it of John, verse 27. In Malachi the messenger precedes the Lord Himself, so applying the line to John carries a quiet claim about who follows him.

Jesus told the Nazareth synagogue that Elijah was sent to a widow in Sidon, and Elisha cleansed Naaman the Syrian, and the crowd tried to kill Him. Chapter 7 shows exactly those two patterns played out: a Gentile centurion is helped, and a widow's son is raised.

Cornelius is another centurion, devout and generous, who is brought into the church after Peter's visit. The centurion of Capernaum is the first of the type in Luke, and Cornelius is the second. Together they show that the good news crosses the boundary between Jew and Gentile.

In Matthew's version of the centurion story Jesus says that many will come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. This opens the larger point that Gentile faith is not an exception, but a sign of the kingdom's final table.

The father in the parable of the lost son sees his son far off and is filled with compassion. Luke uses the same verb as at Nain. The word ties Jesus' mercy to the character of the Father whom He reveals, and it presents the compassion of God as a person who runs.

The tax collector who will not lift his eyes and prays for mercy goes home justified, while the Pharisee does not. Simon and the sinful woman are the same pair in a different scene, and Luke wants readers to see that the outcome rests on humility and not on reputation.

study.oneStory:
Genesis ended with a family in a coffin in Egypt, and the Old Testament goes on to ask what can reverse death and what can cancel a debt that no one can pay. Luke 7 stands in the line of answers. Elijah and Elisha were given back a son each. Isaiah promised that the dead would live and that a day of release would come. Malachi said a messenger would clear the road for the Lord Himself. Here these separate hopes land in a single village road, and in the same ministry.

Notice who is made ready for that. A Gentile soldier, a grieving widow, a prisoner who is plagued by doubt and a woman known only by her sin: they are the people the prophets said would be gathered, the poor and the captives and the brokenhearted. And the people best placed to recognise the moment, the lawyers and the Pharisee at his table, are the ones who miss it. Luke is preparing for the way the whole story will turn out, with the cross proving that no one is righteous and the resurrection opening the way to forgiven sinners from every nation.

The chapter also gestures forward. The woman's weeping at Jesus' feet is answered at the end of the Gospel by another group of women who come with spices to a tomb, Luke 24:1, and find that the One they came to anoint has risen. The 'peace' with which He sends her away is the peace that He will speak to the disciples after the resurrection, Luke 24:36. And the question 'Who is this who even forgives sins?' is answered by the commission of Luke 24:47, that repentance and forgiveness of sins would be preached in His name to all nations.

The story ends in the new creation where the greatest in the kingdom stand and where debts are no more. Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear, and the woman who wet His feet with her tears is a first sign. The dead son of Nain, given back to his mother, is a sign that the final resurrection will not be an escape from the world but its renewal. Every miracle in Luke 7 is a preview of the day when He says to the dead what He said at the gate, and all of them sit up.

sermon.title: The Sinful Woman
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Luke, this message on Luke 7:36 walks through the sinful woman who anointed Jesus' feet, showing how forgiveness received produces overflowing love, and that only Jesus can tell us our sins are forgiven. A faithful, expository treatment of this movement's climactic scene.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus marvel at the centurion?

options.text: Because his faith rested wholly on Jesus' word, a greater faith than Jesus had found in Israel.
options.note: Luke 7:9 records Jesus' amazement at the centurion's trust that Jesus need only speak.

options.text: Because the centurion had built a synagogue and loved the Jewish nation.
options.note: True of the man, and cited by the elders, but Jesus marveled specifically at his faith, not his good works.

options.text: Because he was a powerful Roman officer worth honoring.
options.note: His rank is not the point; the centurion himself felt unworthy, and Jesus praised his faith.

options.text: Because he demanded that Jesus prove Himself.
options.note: The centurion did the opposite, humbly trusting Jesus' word without needing Him to come.

quiz.q: What moved Jesus to raise the widow's son at Nain?

options.text: His deep compassion for the grieving widow, whom He comforted and whose son He gave back alive.
options.note: Luke 7:13 says the Lord had compassion on her and acted before being asked.

options.text: The large crowd accompanying the funeral procession.
options.note: A crowd was present, but Jesus was moved by compassion for the widow, not by the audience.

options.text: A request from the widow for a miracle.
options.note: She did not ask; Jesus acted first, out of His own compassion.

options.text: A desire to prove He was more powerful than Herod.
options.note: The scene is about mercy and Jesus' identity, not a contest with Herod.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer John the Baptist's question about His identity?

options.text: By pointing to His works: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news.
options.note: Luke 7:22 has Jesus cite the Isaiah-shaped works of salvation as His answer.

options.text: By simply declaring that He was the Messiah.
options.note: He does affirm His identity, but He does it by pointing to the works that fulfill Isaiah, not by a bare claim.

options.text: By rebuking John sharply for his doubt.
options.note: Jesus does not rebuke John; He answers gently and then praises John as more than a prophet.

options.text: By refusing to answer the question at all.
options.note: Jesus gives a clear, evidence-based answer to John's messengers.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the two debtors teach about the sinful woman?

options.text: The one forgiven a greater debt loves more, so her great love flows from being forgiven much.
options.note: Luke 7:41-47 makes forgiveness the cause and love the grateful response.

options.text: Her lavish love was the visible proof that she had already been forgiven.
options.note: A fair reading of 'she loved much' as evidence, but the parable's logic still puts forgiveness first as the cause.

options.text: Her love earned her forgiveness by outweighing her sins.
options.note: This reverses the parable; Jesus finally says her faith, not her love, saved her.

options.text: She was forgiven because she was less sinful than Simon thought.
options.note: Jesus calls her sins many; she is forgiven much, not shown to be a minor sinner.

quiz.q: What did Jesus finally say had saved the woman?

options.text: Her faith; 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
options.note: Luke 7:50 grounds her salvation in faith, received by trusting Jesus.

options.text: Her tears and her costly perfume poured on His feet.
options.note: These expressed her devotion, but Jesus names faith, not her acts, as what saved her.

options.text: Her willingness to face the scorn of the onlookers.
options.note: Her boldness was real, but it was faith in Jesus, not her courage, that saved her.

options.text: Simon's willingness to host Jesus at his table.
options.note: Simon is contrasted with the woman; his hospitality did nothing to save her.

questions: The centurion trusted that Jesus need only speak the word. Where do you need to rest more simply on what Jesus has said, rather than on what you can see or manage?
At Nain Jesus was moved with compassion for a grieving widow and acted before she asked. How does it comfort you to know that Jesus sees your grief and cares deeply about it?
John the Baptist, faithful yet struggling in prison, honestly brought his doubt to Jesus. What doubt or question do you need to bring to Jesus rather than carry alone?
The woman loved much because she had been forgiven much. Does your love for Christ reflect a deep sense of how much you have been forgiven, and where might that sense have grown cold?
Simon judged the woman while missing his own need; Jesus welcomed her. Where are you tempted to look down on 'sinners' rather than to see yourself as one who has also been forgiven?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered coffin is literally a bier, an open plank or frame on which the body was carried, so Jesus touches the funeral bier rather than a closed casket.
A denarius was a day's wage for a laborer, so five hundred denarii was well over a year's pay; the sizes of the two debts sharpen the point about forgiveness and love.

The phrase 'her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much' is read alongside the parable, where forgiveness is the cause and love the response, so that faith, named in verse 50, is what saves.
